**Backend:**
- **`GET /api/digest/status`** (`api/digest.py`) returns:

  - `scored_today` / `daily_score_cap`;
  - `can_refresh`, `refresh_available_at` (from a 30-minute cooldown on the person's last refresh);
  - `over_budget`.
- **Last refresh time** goes in the per-person setting `last_refresh_at`, so it survives restarts and needs no migration.
- **`POST /api/digest/refresh/stream`** checks the cooldown and returns 429 with "You can refresh again in N minutes" when it applies. Otherwise it records `last_refresh_at` and starts `start_run_daily(only_user=me, fresh_hours=1)`, streaming exactly like `/api/pipeline/run-daily/stream`. The SSE loop is factored out of `api/pipeline.py` into a shared helper.
- **Skip sources fetched in the last hour:**
  - a new `fresh_hours` parameter threads through `run_daily` → `_run_daily` → `_poll_sources`;

  - `_run_for_person` still queues and scores that person's jobs from those sources, using the jobs already stored (a new `_recent_jobs_for_sources(source_ids)`: active jobs of those sources seen in the last day), so a second person refreshing right after the first still gets scored;
  - this also covers jobs already found by someone else's run today.
- **When the cap is used up:** the run still fetches, and the summary carries `cap_reached: true`, so the page can say "Scoring resumes tomorrow (20 of 20 used today)".
- "Check my sources now" on Manage Sources keeps working as-is, with no cooldown. It's rarely used, and the daily cap and budget already bound its cost. Refresh is the main way in.

- **When the cap or budget is reached,** show "Scoring resumes tomorrow (20 of 20 used today)" or the budget message under the line.

## Step 4, cost controls — DONE (deployed)

**Already in place from steps 2-3:**
- each person's daily cap (`users.daily_score_cap`, `daily_run.remaining_cap()`);
- `last_seen_at`, updated hourly by `users.touch_last_seen()` from `api/auth.py`;
- spend per person in `llm_calls.user_id`;
- `email_digest.send_plain_email()` and `admin_address()`.

**1. Score only people active in the last 7 days.**
- `core/users.py`: `ACTIVE_DAYS = 7` and `active_user_ids()`.
  - Active means approved and `COALESCE(last_seen_at, decided_at, created_at)` within 7 days, so a brand-new or just-migrated person counts until their first visit.
  - It replaces `approved_user_ids()` in `daily_run._run_daily()` for the everyone run.
  - Polling then reads only sources followed by active people (`_poll_sources(user_ids=people)` already does this).
  - `only_user` runs ("Check my sources now", onboarding) are unaffected, since that person is active by definition.
- **The paused email** (`daily_run._send_paused_emails()`, called in the everyone run):
  - for each approved, inactive person with `paused_email_sent_at IS NULL`, send one email and set `paused_email_sent_at`;
  - wording: "Your daily job matches are paused because you haven't opened the app in a week. Open it to pick them back up: <APP_URL>";
  - a send that fails or isn't configured leaves the column NULL so it retries next run;
  - `touch_last_seen()` clears `paused_email_sent_at` in the same UPDATE that records the visit.
- The admin is subject to the same rule; there's no exemption, since the admin visits anyway.

**2. Monthly budget per person.**
- New `core/budget.py`:
  - `spend_this_month(user_id)` sums `llm_calls.estimated_cost_usd` since `date('now','start of month')`;
  - `status(user_id)` returns `{spend, budget, remaining, over, exempt}`;
  - `class BudgetExceeded(LLMError)` carries a plain message: "You've used your $10.00 Claude budget for this month. It resets on Dec 1, or the admin can raise it."
- **Enforcement at one choke point:** `core/llm.py`'s `get_client()`, which every paid call site calls right before calling Claude (17 sites). When a person is set (`optional_user_id()`), isn't an admin, and is at or over budget, it raises `BudgetExceeded`.
  - Because it's an `LLMError`, every route already turns it into a clean error message, and the pipeline catches it per job.
  - Shared work (nobody set) is never blocked.
  - **The admin is exempt:** it's their own key and money. Their spend still shows.
- **Daily run:** `_run_for_person()` skips scoring (allowed = 0) when the budget is used up, rather than failing job by job, and the summary notes "budget reached".
- **Alerts to the admin, once per person per month:**
  - in `log_call()`, after the insert, when a non-admin person's month spend crosses 80% of their budget, and again at 100%;
  - tracked by two new `users` columns, `budget_alert_month` and `budget_block_month` (e.g. '2026-11'), added via `MIGRATIONS` ALTERs, since the live `users` table exists already;
  - the email reads e.g. "Bea has used $8.10 of their $10 Claude budget this month. Change it on /admin";
  - a failure never breaks the call.
- **Budget shown to the person:**
  - `GET /api/me` adds `usage: {spend_this_month, monthly_budget_usd, exempt, scored_today, daily_score_cap}`;
  - Settings' Usage card shows "This month: $3.20 of your $10.00 budget · Today: 12 of 20 jobs scored" (admin: "no limit");
  - the Admin page already shows spend against budget, so its "enforcement comes next" note is removed.

- `src/jobhunt/pipeline/daily_run.py`, `src/jobhunt/db/connection.py` (MIGRATIONS) + `schema.sql` (the new columns)

## Status (2026-11-02)
- **Step 1 is built, pushed and deployed.** After the deploy:
  - `gs://…/litestream/jobhunt/generations/eb572992fc7209d4/snapshots/` exists;
  - the `litestream-seeded` marker reads `2026-11-02T20:58:18Z`.

  Still to confirm: the snapshot and WAL files exist (the `| head` cut off the listing), and My Jobs looks right in the app.

## Step 1: Reliability: SQLite plus Litestream (useful even for one user) — DONE
- **The database moves onto the container's own disk** (`JOBHUNT_DB_PATH=/tmp/db/jobhunt.db`). Litestream replicates every change to `gs://…-jobhunt-data/litestream/` within about a second.
  - The image entrypoint becomes `litestream restore -if-replica-exists` then `litestream replicate -exec "uvicorn …"`. Litestream runs the app as its child process and flushes on shutdown.
  - `litestream.yml` goes in the repo; the Dockerfile gets the Litestream binary.
- **One-time move:** the first start finds no replica, so it seeds from the existing `/data/jobhunt.db` on the bucket mount, then replicates from then on. The old file stays as a fallback.
- **Documents (`resumes/`) stay on the bucket mount.** They're written rarely and whole, which suits it.
- **The daily snapshots (`core/backup.py`) keep running,** pointed at the local database, written to `/data/backups/` on the bucket. They're a second layer of protection on top of Litestream.
- **Cloud Run settings:**
  - the CPU stays on while the server runs (`--no-cpu-throttling`), so replication never stalls between requests;
  - memory goes to 2 GiB for headless-browser board reading;
  - still `--max-instances 1` and min instances 0.

  With sparse use the server still shuts down after about 15 idle minutes.
- **Tests and checks:**
  - a local run with Litestream pointed at a temp folder: write, kill, restore, data intact;
  - restore, then confirm the app sees the same applications;
  - the snapshot code works with the new path.
- **Docs:** CLAUDE.md Deploy section, D-020.

## Step 2: Per-person data (the largest step)
- **New `users` table:** `id`, `email` (unique), `name`, `status` (pending / approved / blocked), `is_admin`, `daily_score_cap` (20), `monthly_budget_usd` (10), `last_seen_at`, `paused_email_sent_at`, `created_at`.
  - You are seeded as user 1 and admin.
  - All existing rows migrate to user 1, through a one-time migration, with a snapshot taken first (`backup.snapshot("before-migration")`).
- **`user_id` (NOT NULL, indexed) on every per-person table:**
  - `candidate_profile`, `preference_profile`, `settings` (key becomes (user_id, key)), `resumes`, `generated_documents`;
  - `applications`, `application_status_history`, `feedback`, `job_scores`, `scoring_queue`, `digest_entries`;
  - `jobby_threads` (uniqueness becomes per user + job), `llm_calls`, `runs`.
- **Sources are shared:**
  - `sources` stays global, deduplicated by URL or board token;
  - a new `source_follows (user_id, source_id)` records who follows what;
  - Manage Sources shows only the boards and organizations you follow, and "Add" or "Monitor" follows an existing source if one matches;
  - deleting a source stops following it, and removes the source itself only when nobody follows it any more.

  `jobs` stays shared for source jobs. Pasted-in jobs carry an owner (`jobs.user_id`, nullable) and are private.
- **Code:**
  - A FastAPI dependency, `current_user()`, gives every route the signed-in user. Every core function takes a `user_id`, and every query filters on it.
  - Files are stored per person: `resumes/<user_id>/…`.
  - Settings that apply to everyone (email sender, prompt-cache stats) stay global; per-person ones move to the per-user settings.
- **Daily run:**
  - fetch every source followed by at least one active user, once;
  - prefilter and score per user, round-robin across users, each within their remaining daily cap;
  - digest and email per user.

  The `_run_lock` and progress tracking become aware of who triggered a run.
- **Isolation tests:** a parameterized test signs in as user A and user B. B must get 404/403 or empty results from every endpoint touching A's data: lists, details, downloads, the CSV export, Jobby, documents, settings and insights.

## Step 3: Sign-in, approval and admin
- **IAP lets any Google account through** (`allAuthenticatedUsers`, via a new `make iap-open` target you run).
- **Middleware verifies `x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion`** (signature, audience, expiry, using Google's public keys, cached) and maps the email to a user.
  - Unknown email: a "Request access" page (name plus an optional note) creates a `pending` user and emails you a link to the admin page.
  - Pending users see a "Waiting for approval" page; blocked users see "No access".
  - Every `/api/*` route except the access-request ones requires an approved user.
  - Locally and in tests, a dev setting stands in for IAP, with a fixed signed test token; a plain header is never trusted.
- **Admin page** (`/admin`, admins only):
  - pending requests with Approve and Decline, each emailing the person;
  - users with status, last visit, scored today against their cap, spend this month against their budget, and editable cap and budget;
  - a Block switch, and a count of sources each person follows.
- **"Check every source now"** on Manage Sources becomes admin-only, since it runs the check for everyone.

## Step 4: Cost controls
- **Active users only:** the daily run scores and emails only users with `last_seen_at` within 7 days. Any authenticated page load updates `last_seen_at`, throttled to once an hour.
- **The "paused" email:** sent once, the first daily run after someone passes 7 days ("Your daily matches are paused. Open the app to pick them back up," with a link).
  - Tracked by `paused_email_sent_at`, which clears on their next visit. Coming back resumes scoring at the next run, or right away via Refresh.
- **Per-person daily cap** replaces the global `daily_llm_cap`, shared by the daily run and Refresh.
- **Per-person monthly budget:**
  - summed from that user's `llm_calls` for this month;
  - at 80% you get an email (once per user per month);
  - at 100%, paid actions (Jobby, tailoring, discovery, "Ask Jobby", Refresh's scoring, the daily scoring) stop with a clear message until the budget is raised or the month rolls over;
  - a one-line "budget used" indicator on the user's Settings.
- **Prompt caching stays per user** (the scoring context is identical within one user's batch), so step 2's round-robin scores each user's jobs as one contiguous batch to keep the cache warm.

## Step 5: New & Noteworthy freshness
- **"Last updated 2 hours ago"** from the user's latest finished check, daily or refresh, from the per-user `runs` table.
- **A "Refresh" button** that runs this person's check now:
  - fetches their followed sources, skipping any fetched by anyone in the last hour;
  - scores within what's left of today's cap;
  - adds to their New & Noteworthy.

  It streams progress like the existing check ("Reading 3 of 8 sources… Scored 5 of 12…") and has a 30-minute cooldown per person.
- **When today's cap is used up,** it still fetches new postings and says "scoring resumes tomorrow (20 of 20 used today)".
- **A user coming back after a pause** sees "Last updated 9 days ago · Refresh" as the prominent prompt.

## Step 6: Email and trust
- **The daily email goes to each person's own address** (their sign-in email), from your Gmail via the existing SMTP set-up (500/day limit; fine for 20). The approval, paused and budget emails use the same path.
- **"Delete my account"** on Settings: types DELETE, takes a snapshot, then removes all of that user's rows and files and their follows. Sources nobody follows any more are removed.
  - The admin can delete a user the same way.
- **Privacy note** shown on the request-access page and linked in Settings: what's stored, that resume text, profile and postings go to Anthropic's API, and that the user can delete everything.

## Cost picture (estimated)

| | Per month |
|---|---|
| Cloud Run, storage, Litestream | about $2–8 |
| Claude, each active person with defaults | about $5–20, capped at their budget |
| Claude, each inactive person | $0 |
| Worst case, 20 people all at budget | $200 |

## Order and deploys
- **Step 1 ships first,** on its own; you notice nothing but better safety.
- **Steps 2 and 3 ship together,** since per-user data needs an identity. Until you approve someone, it's still just you.
- **Step 4 then 5 then 6;** each deploys separately.
- **Invite people after step 4.** Steps 5 and 6 can follow while a few people are using it.

## Verification throughout
- Every step: pytest gated on its exit status, ruff, the frontend build, and a browser walk-through on the stub server, with two signed test identities from step 2 on.
- Step 2: the isolation test suite. Step 1: a restore test.
- Every data migration runs against a copy of a pre-migration snapshot shape in tests before it ships.
- The deploy commands you run (Cloud Shell) are listed per step, including the one-time `make iap-open`.

## ab602548-125 · 2026-11-06 15:05 UTC

**Prompt**

> How much would it cost to keep a warm instance?

**Claude**

Keeping one Job Search Assistant instance warm would cost about **$50–57 a month**.

That's for its current setup: 1 vCPU, 2 GiB of memory, and the CPU always on (`--no-cpu-throttling`). With the CPU always on, Cloud Run bills a warm instance at the full rate all day, whether or not anyone is using it. These are the us-central1 list prices as I last knew them, so check them on Cloud Run's pricing page.

| | Rate | Per month (30 days) |
|---|---|---|
| CPU, 1 vCPU | $0.000018 per vCPU-second | ~$46.70 |
| Memory, 2 GiB | $0.000002 per GiB-second | ~$10.40 |
| **Total** | | **~$57** |
| Less the monthly free allowance | | about $5 off, so ~$52, if Shelf Life isn't already using it |

The free allowance is shared across your billing account. Shelf Life already keeps a warm instance, so it has probably used it up, which puts this nearer $57.

**Compared with now:** at minimum 0 instances, the server shuts down about 15 minutes after the last visit. You pay only while it's running: the 2pm check, plus whenever someone is using it. That's likely a few dollars a month. The cost of that is a slow first load after it's been idle: the large image with the browser has to start, and the database has to be restored from Cloud Storage.

**A cheaper warm instance isn't a good fit here.** If the CPU were switched to "only during requests", a warm instance would bill at the idle rate, about $19 a month. But the database's copy to Cloud Storage (Litestream) needs the CPU between requests. Without it, recent changes could be lost if the server stopped. I'd keep the CPU always on.

**Middle options:**
- **Warm only during the day**, for example 8am–10pm Eastern. A scheduled job would switch the minimum between 1 and 0. That's about $33 a month, at the cost of a little more to set up.
- **Make the cold start faster instead.** Cloud Run's startup CPU boost speeds startup at almost no cost. Trimming the image would help too.

My suggestion: with a handful of occasional users, I'd try the startup boost first and switch to a warm instance only if the wait on first load still bothers you. If you'd rather have one, it's a one-line Makefile change (`--min-instances 1`) plus a deploy, and I can make it.

## ab602548-126 · 2026-11-06 15:07 UTC

**Prompt**

> <!-- attach -->
> > Make the cold start faster instead. Cloud Run’s startup CPU boost speeds startup at almost no cost. Trimming the image would help too.
>
> Say more about this

**Claude**

A cold start currently has four stages. In rough order of how much time they likely cost:

1. **Starting the container.** Cloud Run fetches the image, mounts the Cloud Storage folder (`data/`), and boots the second-generation environment. The image is large, mostly because of Chromium, which the browser fallback for some job boards needs.
2. **Restoring the database.** Before the app starts, `start.sh` has Litestream copy the database down from Cloud Storage. It takes a full snapshot only once a day (`snapshot-interval: 24h`). After that it saves changes as many small files, each a separate download. The 2pm check writes a lot, so a morning visit could mean replaying close to a day of them.
3. **Python importing the app.** That takes 1.3 seconds here. On Cloud Run's single vCPU it's probably 2–4 seconds. About half of it is the Anthropic SDK, which is loaded at startup even though nothing calls Claude until later.
4. **Startup work.** `init_db()` runs, then `backfill_salaries()` scans every active job still missing a salary, before the first request is served.

**What each fix would do:**
- **Startup CPU boost** (`--cpu-boost` on deploy). Cloud Run gives the instance extra CPU while it starts, which speeds up stages 3 and 4. It costs a few cents a month (extra CPU only for those seconds) and is a one-line Makefile change. This is the easy win.
- **Hourly Litestream snapshots** (`snapshot-interval: 1h`). A restore then replays at most an hour of changes instead of up to a day. It costs pennies in storage, and the week of point-in-time restore stays. For the biggest variable, the database restore, it's probably the best fix after the boost.
- **Run the salary backfill in the background,** so the first page doesn't wait for it, and **load the Anthropic and Playwright libraries only when they're first used.** That saves about a second, maybe two. It's a small code change with tests.
- **Trimming the image.** This helps less than people expect, because Cloud Run streams images rather than downloading them whole. The only big piece is Chromium, which the job-board fallback needs. Moving it to a separate service would add a lot of complexity, so I wouldn't.

**Measure first.** I can't time a real cold start from here. The Cloud Run logs record how long the instance took to start, and the `start.sh` lines show when the restore finished. One look after a cold start (open the app after 15+ idle minutes) would show where the seconds go.

I'd suggest the boost, hourly snapshots and the background backfill together. That's about $0 a month extra, against about $52 for a warm instance. My guess is it would take several seconds off a cold start; I can't promise a number without the measurement. Shall I make those changes? They'd go on the `projects` branch, since that's where the code lives now.

**Why it failed:** Civic Work Studio runs on WP Job Manager, a common WordPress plugin for job boards. Its page arrives with an empty job list, and a script on the page then loads the jobs a few at a time. So when the app read the page, even in its headless browser, it found at most the first handful of the board's 362 jobs. techjobsforgov.com, one of your sources, now serves the same board, so it had the same problem.

**The fix:** when a page uses that plugin, the app now asks the plugin directly for its job list instead of reading the page.
- **All jobs:** it reads every job, 100 per request, up to 500 per board.
- **Your filters:** the filters in your URL (remote only, the job types) still apply.
- **No cost:** there's no Claude call, so reading these boards is now free.
- **Details:** each job comes with title, organization, location, posted date and the pay shown on the card.

Run live from here, your filtered URL returned the same **30 remote jobs** the site shows, and techjobsforgov.com returned **362**. If the plugin's list ever can't be read, the app goes back to reading the page as before. All 488 tests pass, including 9 new ones.

**Two things to know:**
- **More jobs to choose from:** these boards will now supply many more jobs. Scoring still stops at your daily cap, and the rest wait their turn.
- **This only fixes boards built on WP Job Manager.** If other boards are failing, send me a couple of their links, or what "Test fetch" on Manage Sources shows for them, and I'll check what they run on.

I found and fixed one real gap in the location dealbreaker; it's pushed to the branch. I can't see your production data from here, though, so I can't yet confirm it's what let those particular jobs into your email.

**What I checked:** I ran about 30 common ways of writing New York and San Francisco locations through the rule, with "DC" as your location. Most were correctly hidden. A few slipped through:
- **Work-arrangement notes:** "New York City, NY (Hybrid)" was read as two places, "New York City" and an unreadable "NY (Hybrid)". The rule keeps any job with an unreadable place, so it survived. "San Francisco, CA - In Office" failed the same way.
- **"SF" on its own** wasn't recognized as San Francisco.

**The fix:** words like "(Hybrid)", "On-site:" and "- In Office" are now ignored when reading a location. "SF" counts as San Francisco. A DC job marked hybrid still matches.

New & Noteworthy and the email use the same check, and a new test confirms the email leaves out a hidden New York or San Francisco job. All 501 tests pass.

**Other reasons a job can still get through:** these are intentional, but they'd explain your email if the fix above doesn't.
1. **The dealbreaker is off.** "Only show jobs in these locations" has to be checked under Profile → "What are you looking for?". Without it, your locations only guide scoring.
2. **The job is marked remote** by its source, or its location text says "remote". Remote jobs are always kept.
3. **No location was listed.** Unknown locations are always kept.

To see which applied, run this in Cloud Shell. It reads your latest daily backup, so an email sent today may not show up in it yet:

```bash
F=$(gsutil ls gs://job-searcher-512814-jobhunt-data/backups/ | grep -v before | sort | tail -1) && gsutil -q cp "$F" /tmp/jh.db && sqlite3 -header -column /tmp/jh.db "SELECT key, value FROM settings WHERE user_id = 1 AND key IN ('location_dealbreaker', 'prefilter_locations'); SELECT substr(de.emailed_at, 1, 16) AS emailed, j.title, j.location, j.remote_type FROM digest_entries de JOIN jobs j ON j.id = de.job_id WHERE de.user_id = 1 AND de.emailed_at >= date('now', '-5 days') ORDER BY de.emailed_at;" ; rm -f /tmp/jh.db
```

It prints your two location settings, then each recently emailed job with its location and remote marking. Send me the output and I'll tell you which reason applied.

The warm window is set up and pushed to the branch: every day from 9:30am to 8:30pm Eastern, which I estimate at about **$26 a month** from list prices. That's half the cost of keeping it warm all day. Outside those hours the app starts on demand, as now.

**How it works:**

- **No redeploys:** nothing about the service changes twice a day, so there's no restart overlap where a change could be lost.
- **Your activity:** the pings don't count as you visiting, so they don't affect the 7-day "active user" rule for scoring.
- **Scheduler cost:** one cron line can't start and stop at half past, so it takes three jobs. With your 2pm job that's four, one more than Google's three free, so about 10¢ a month.

## ab602548-158 · 2026-11-11 13:36 UTC

**Prompt**

> if I'm away from the site for a long time and then go back and click the Manage Sources / All Jobs / My Jobs / New & Noteworthy pages, all the data will be gone until I refresh. Is that expected? If so, is there a UI feature we can add so users know their data isn't gone and they just need to refresh?

**Claude**

It wasn't expected; it was a bug, and I've fixed it on the branch. You now get a clear message instead of empty pages.

**Why it happened:** the app sits behind Google's sign-in (IAP), and that session runs out after some time away. When you came back, the page you had open asked the server for data in the background, and Google answered by sending those requests to its sign-in page. A background request can't follow that, so it failed, and the pages showed nothing. A refresh is a full page load, which goes through sign-in properly. Your data was never affected.

**What changed:**
- **Expired sessions are recognized.** Every request the app makes now carries a marker that tells Google's sign-in layer it comes from the page's own code, so Google answers "signed out" instead of redirecting. If a request fails anyway, the app checks once more before blaming your connection.
- **A banner instead of empty pages:** "You've been signed out after some time away. Reload the page to sign back in — your data is safe." It has a Reload button and stays fixed at the bottom of the screen.
- **A check as soon as you return.** If the tab was hidden for more than 5 minutes, the app checks your session right away, so the banner can appear before you click into a page.

**How I tested it:** I imitated an expired session in a browser, both as a clean "signed out" answer and as a redirect to Google's sign-in page. Either way the banner appeared when I opened Manage Sources, and normal page loads showed no banner. I couldn't test against Google's real sign-in from here. After you deploy, leaving the tab open for an hour or two and coming back is the real test. If the banner doesn't show up then, tell me.

To deploy:

```bash
cd ~/projects/"01 - Claude Code Projects/02 - Job Search Assistant" && git checkout main && git pull && git merge origin/claude/move-job-search-assistant && git push && make deploy ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com
```

**A possible next step:** Google also documents a way for the page to refresh the sign-in itself, so you might not need to reload at all. It's less reliable, because it depends on browser pop-up and cookie settings, so I started with the banner. It's worth adding if reloading gets annoying.

Sources:
- [Managing IAP sessions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/sessions-howto?no_redirect=true)
- [Managing sessions with external identities](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/external-identity-sessions?authuser=5)

## ab602548-167 · 2026-11-11 16:39 UTC

**Prompt**

> How do we handle a user with only PDF resumes/cover letters?

**Claude**

A user with only PDFs can do everything except get a formatted Word file back. Tailored resumes and cover letters come back as plain text, and they download as a `.md` file.

**What works the same as with Word files**
- **Upload and text extraction.** Both upload pickers accept `.pdf`, `.docx`, `.md` and `.txt`. The PDF's text is read out with pypdf (`core/resume_parse.py`), and only that text is used everywhere else.
- **Everything built from that text:**
  - the candidate profile;
  - scoring;
  - discovery;
  - Jobby, which gets the documents' text in its context.

**What's different: tailoring** (`core/generate.py`)
- **Resume.** A `.docx` resume gets your exact edits written into your own file as Word tracked changes, so the formatting is untouched. That's impossible with a PDF: `_usable_template_path()` returns nothing for a non-`.docx` file. So `_generate_resume_plain()` instead asks Claude to rewrite the whole resume as Markdown, from the PDF's text plus the profile.
- **Cover letter.** Without a `.docx` cover letter, `_generate_cover_letter_plain()` writes a fresh letter from the profile and the job only. It never sees the person's own past letter, so it can't match their voice or structure.
- **Download.** No Word file is saved. The download serves the Markdown text as a `.md` file (`api/generate.py`), and the job page says "Not saved as a formatted file (no usable .docx template found…)".

**What the user is told**
- **Onboarding** says up front that a Word file works best and that with a PDF they'd only get plain text back.
- **The Profile page** doesn't repeat that warning, so someone who uploads later only finds out after tailoring.

**Gaps worth fixing, if you want them**
1. **Use the PDF cover letter as a sample.** The plain path could include the existing letter's text as a style and voice reference. That's a small prompt change.
2. **Better downloads.** A `.md` file is awkward for most people. We could build a simple, cleanly formatted `.docx` from the Markdown (no Claude call) so they still get a Word file, just not in their own layout.
3. **A hint on the Profile page.** When the current resume or cover letter is a PDF, say that uploading the Word version gets tailored edits in your own formatting.
4. **Scanned PDFs.** A PDF that's just page images has no text, so the profile would be built from almost nothing, with no warning. We should flag uploads that come back with very little text and ask for another format.

I'd do 1 to 3 together; they're cheap. Want me to go ahead?

**What visitors get**
- **The persona:** a fictional job seeker, "Jordan Rivera", an analytics leader looking at civic tech and public health. Every organization, posting, link and email address is made up.

- I didn't hand-write the fake data in the frontend. A script fills a throwaway database with the fictional content using the app's own code, runs the real app on it, and records its answer to every page request. The published site plays those answers back in the browser.

Now each daily check updates them, so this job and others like it are fixed at the next 2pm check. A posting that comes back with no location doesn't wipe the one already stored.

## ab602548-193 · 2026-11-12 15:04 UTC

**Prompt**

> Give me a breakdown of costs in a scoring run. It seems like we need to find a way to make it cheaper

**Claude**

A scoring run costs about **0.9¢ per job**. With your daily cap of 50, that's about **$0.45 a day**, or roughly $13–14 a month on scoring alone. Here is where a typical job's 0.9¢ goes, averaged over the 10 scoring calls in your screenshot (Sonnet 5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output):

| Part of the call | Tokens | Cost | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| The job posting (new text each call) | ~2,240 | 0.45¢ | **50%** |
| Your profile and preferences (cached, read at 10% of the price) | 5,101 | 0.10¢ | 11% |
| Claude's answer (its reasoning plus the ratings and rationale) | ~355 | 0.35¢ | **39%** |

What that tells us:
- **Caching is already doing its job.** Your 5,100-token context costs a tenth of what it would uncached, so there's little left to gain there.
- **The cost is mostly the posting and the answer.** We already tried trimming those in the scoring experiment (lower effort, a shorter rationale, postings cut at 6,000 characters). It only saved about 10% (0.9¢ → 0.8¢), so tweaks to the call itself won't get us far.
- **The big lever is how many jobs get scored.** You have about 1,700 jobs waiting, so the 50-a-day cap is reached every day, and cost stays at cap × price no matter how well jobs are picked. Many of those jobs are obviously not for you, like Harvey's legal-engineering and sales roles. Scoring them in full spends money on a foregone conclusion.

The options, in the order I'd do them:

1. **Batch processing for the 2pm run: about 50% off, no change in quality.** Anthropic's batch API charges half price for requests that can wait, usually minutes and at most 24 hours. The scheduled run isn't urgent, and caching still works inside a batch. The trade-off is that the daily email goes out when the batch finishes, usually a little later than now. Refresh and "Check my sources now" stay instant at the normal price. This is about $6–7 a month saved at your current volume.
2. **Screen titles before scoring: score fewer, better-chosen jobs.** One cheap call per run reads the waiting jobs' titles and organizations, and sets aside the clear mismatches before any full scoring. It costs a fraction of a cent for hundreds of titles. Your cap then goes to plausible jobs only, which means you could lower it to 20–25 without missing good ones. Combined with option 1, scoring would run about $2–3 a month. The risk is a good job wrongly set aside, so screened-out jobs would stay visible on All Jobs, marked "screened out".
3. **Strip boilerplate from postings: maybe 10–20% off.** Equal-opportunity statements, benefits lists and privacy notices are half of some postings, and the scorer doesn't need them. It's free and deterministic, but a modest saving.
4. **A smaller model for scoring.** Possibly half again, but ratings might get worse. I'd only do this after measuring it with the scoring experiment on the Admin page, the way we tested the lean settings.

One more thing to check: reading job boards is **shared** spend, so it doesn't appear in your personal Usage log. It shows on the Admin page. Each Claude-read board page can cost a few cents, so if the Admin page's shared total is large, that's worth trimming too (the remembered-board fix already helps).

I'd do options 1 and 2 together. Want me to go ahead with those, or start with just the batch processing?

## ab602548-194 · 2026-11-12 15:09 UTC

**Prompt**

> let's do 1 and 2

**Claude**

Both changes are built and pushed to `claude/move-job-search-assistant`.

**1. Batch scoring for the 2pm run (half price)**
- **What changed:** the scheduled check, and "Check every source now", send their scoring to Anthropic's batch service, which charges half price for every token. The prompt, ratings and caching are the same as before; only the price and delivery change.
- **Timing:** batches usually finish in a few minutes. Each run allows them 18 minutes in total, which keeps it inside the scheduler's 30-minute limit. Past that, the batch is cancelled, its finished scores are kept, and the rest are scored the normal way. Jobs the batch reported as failed are scored the normal way too.
- **The daily email** goes out once scoring is done, so it may arrive a few minutes later than before.
- **Your own "Check my sources now" and New & Noteworthy's Refresh** still score immediately, at full price, since you're waiting on them.
- **Usage log:** these calls show as "scoring (batch)" at their halved cost.

**2. A title screen before scoring**
- **What changed:** before any run scores, the waiting jobs' titles, organizations and locations go to Claude Haiku 5.5, about 150 per call. It sets aside only clear mismatches: a different line of work, or far too junior or senior. It's told to keep anything uncertain, and never to judge location, pay or organization.
- **Cost:** very small, about $0.10 per million input tokens, so a few hundredths of a cent per 150 jobs. It shows in the Usage log as "Title screen".
- **Set-aside jobs:** they're never scored, so your daily cap goes to plausible jobs. They're hidden on All Jobs behind a new "Show N jobs set aside by title" toggle. If you show them, their cards say why they weren't scored, and you can still track any of them.
- **Your backlog:** about 1,500 waiting jobs get screened per run, so it's cleared within the first couple of checks.

**Expected effect:** the scheduled run's scoring drops from about $0.45 a day to about $0.23 a day. The bigger saving comes from lowering your daily cap. Once the screen is weeding out mismatches, about 20–25 scored jobs a day should cover the plausible ones. At 20 batched jobs a day, scoring would run roughly $3 a month instead of $13–14. The cap is "Max jobs scored per day" in Settings, and I didn't change it. One thing I couldn't test from here is how strict Haiku is on your real jobs: watch the "set aside by title" count after the first run, and peek at a few. If good jobs are being set aside, tell me and I'll loosen the instructions.

All 571 tests pass, including new ones for the screen, the batch (including the time-out and failure fallbacks), and the half-price logging. This is recorded as decision D-034, milestone M25.

## ab602548-207 · 2026-11-12 21:58 UTC

**Prompt**

> It happens sometimes that a job gets duplicated across All Jobs and My Jobs (I think if the user adds a job manually and then it also gets pulled in from a source). Can we merge these by matching on either A) url, B) title & organization, C) description? Tell me what methodology you think makes the most sense

**Claude**

I'd use all three, ranked by how sure each one is, with the description only ever used to break a tie. That's what I built, and it's pushed. All 587 tests pass, including 10 new ones, but I haven't run it against your real data.

**How jobs are matched, most certain first:**
1. **Link: merges automatically.** I don't compare links as plain text. The same Greenhouse job can have three different addresses, and today's link cleanup would treat two different jobs on one careers page as the same. Instead it reads the job board's own job id from the link: Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday, SmartRecruiters. For any other site it uses the address with tracking bits removed.
2. **Title and organization: only when there's exactly one match.** "Sr." counts as "Senior" and "Inc"/"LLC" are ignored. A big employer can post the same title for several teams or cities, so it only merges when exactly one job from your sources fits and the cities don't clearly differ.
3. **Description: only to break a tie.** Pasted text and job-board text are formatted differently, so it never merges anything on its own. It just picks between several same-titled jobs at one organization, and only when the overlap is clear.

When it isn't sure, nothing merges. A wrong merge would move your application onto a different job, which is worse than a leftover duplicate.

**What a merge does:**
- **Which copy stays:** the one from the source, since it's updated daily and closes when the posting comes down.
- **What moves over:** your application, status history, scores, feedback, tailored documents, Jobby chat, and pay or posted date if the source copy is missing them.
- **If both copies are on My Jobs:** the one further along wins, and both sets of notes are kept.

**When it runs:**
- **Duplicates you already have** are merged once when the app starts after the deploy.
- **When a source finds a job you pasted earlier,** it's merged then.
- **When you paste a job a source already has:** a link match is caught before reading the posting with Claude, which saves that call. Pasted text is checked by title and organization after it's read. Either way, that job is put on My Jobs instead of a new copy, and "Add a job" tells you it was already in your sources.

**What it won't catch:** a pasted job with no link whose title is worded differently from the board's. You'd still see both copies.

This needs a deploy:

```bash
cd ~/projects/"01 - Claude Code Projects/02 - Job Search Assistant" && git checkout main && git pull && git merge --no-edit origin/claude/move-job-search-assistant && git push && make deploy ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com IAP_AUDIENCE=/projects/<project number>/locations/us-central1/services/jobhunt
```

Afterwards, the duplicate you noticed should show once on All Jobs, marked with its My Jobs status. If it's still doubled, send me its link or title and I'll check why it didn't match.
